The AR tags on the guardrail and Plug’s GenDrive fuel cell unit were used to measure the truck position relative to the guardrail. The operator then approached the dispenser from three different directions, ten times each, for a total of 30 trials. The operator attempted to drive as quickly as possible to the “home” position without reversing direction or taking great pains to achieve alignment (Figure 2). The error in truck position from the home position was then calculated by the vision system. AR Tag Figure 1: Home position of a Class 3 end-rider. Figure 3 shows the error measurements of each trial in terms of truck angle (yaw about the vertical axis), distance parallel to guardrail and distance perpendicular to guardrail. These measurements were then used to create the range of motion requirements in the System Requirements Document (SRD). Several mechanical design concepts were conceived for an automated dispenser that would provide a reliable, low-cost solution for moving and mating the fueling nozzle to the fueling receptacle. The final concept chosen is a selective compliance articulated robot arm (SCARA)-type mechanism with two arms for horizontal motion and a ball screw for vertical movement (See Figure 4). Servo motors at the shoulder and elbow joints provide a wide range of motion in the horizontal plane while a small servo motor at the wrist adjusts rotation of the nozzle about the vertical axis. A fourth servo motor actuates the cam to lock the nozzle to the receptacle. The nozzle is not required to angle out of the horizontal plane in the AGV application as it can be assumed that the truck is on a flat, level surface and the receptacle is parallel to the ground.
